passages.t: The queen of Babylon brought down to the dust
passages.happening:
‘Go down and sit in the dust, O Virgin Daughter of Babylon’ (verse 1). She is to sit on the ground without a throne. ‘For you will no longer be called tender or delicate’ (verse 1).

She is told to take millstones and grind flour, to remove her veil, strip off her skirt and wade through the streams (verse 2). Her shame will be exposed, and God says, ‘I will take vengeance; I will spare no one’ (verse 3).

Then, in the middle of the poem, Israel breaks in with praise. Their Redeemer, whose name is the LORD of Hosts, is ‘the Holy One of Israel’ (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
Babylon under the Chaldean kings was the greatest city of its day. Nebuchadnezzar II, who ruled from about 605 to 562 BC, rebuilt it on a vast scale, with massive walls, the Ishtar Gate and the temple of Marduk. It was his army that took Jerusalem in 597 BC and destroyed it in 587 or 586 BC.

The poem pictures the city as a pampered royal lady. Royal women lived veiled and carried, in seclusion and luxury. Slave women ground grain by hand between millstones, the lowliest work in a household. To lose the veil and wade through rivers on foot was to be driven into exile as a captive. The picture turns back on Babylon what Babylon had done to the daughters of Judah.

This is a taunt song, a poem mocking a fallen enemy, like the song over the king of Babylon in chapter 14. It is spoken to Babylon throughout, except for verse 4, where Israel's own voice of praise interrupts it.
passages.later: Grinding at the hand mill was the place of the lowest servant, as in the Passover warning about ‘the servant girl behind the hand mill’ (Exodus 11:5). Jesus states the reversal the chapter shows: ‘everyone who exalts himself will be humbled’ (Luke 14:11).
passages.hard:
The poem pictures a city as a woman stripped and shamed. How should a reader take it?

The picture is drawn from the real treatment of captive women in ancient war, the treatment Babylon had dealt to others, and it is turned on the city, which is spoken of as a woman. It is a prophetic picture of a city and an empire brought low. It gives no warrant for any man to shame or harm a woman. The target is the empire, not women, and nothing in this chapter makes the abuse of a woman anything other than evil.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Babylon thought of itself as too delicate ever to grind at a mill. Ask what place in life you think you are above. And ask what it means that Israel's response to Babylon's fall is not gloating but praise of its Redeemer.

passages.t: No mercy shown, and a city that spoke as if it were God
passages.happening:
‘Sit in silence and go into darkness, O Daughter of Chaldea. For you will no longer be called the queen of kingdoms’ (verse 5).

God explains. ‘I was angry with My people; I profaned My heritage, and I placed them under your control’ (verse 6). But Babylon went further. ‘You showed them no mercy; even on the elderly you laid a most heavy yoke’ (verse 6). She thought she would be queen forever and never considered the outcome (verse 7).

So God speaks to the ‘lover of luxury who sits securely’ (verse 8). Babylon tells herself that she alone exists, and that she will never be a widow or lose her children (verse 8). ‘These two things will overtake you in a moment, in a single day: loss of children, and widowhood’ (verse 9), in spite of all her sorceries.

She was secure in her wickedness and thought no one saw her (verse 10). Her wisdom led her astray. ‘But disaster will come upon you; you will not know how to charm it away’ (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
Verse 6 answers a question the first hearers would have asked. If God handed his people to Babylon, why judge Babylon for it? Because Babylon went beyond judgment into cruelty. It showed no mercy, and it laid a heavy yoke even on the old. A nation may be used by God and still answer for its own pride and its own cruelty, as Assyria did in chapter 10.

Widowhood and the loss of children were the two great fears of an ancient woman. Both left her without protection or a future. The city that thought itself beyond loss is told it will meet both in one day.

Twice Babylon claims that she alone exists and there is no other beside her (verses 8 and 10). Those are close to the words God speaks of himself in chapter 45. The city talks as though it were God, and so it falls.

Babylon fell to Cyrus in 539 BC with little resistance. It was not destroyed then and remained a great city under the Persians, but its empire ended at once and never returned.
passages.later: Revelation takes up these verses for the great city opposed to God, which says in her heart that she sits as queen, ‘As much as she has glorified herself and lived in luxury’ (Revelation 18:7). God's own claim stands behind the chapter: ‘I am the LORD, and there is no other’ (Isaiah 45:5).
passages.hard:
If God handed his people to Babylon, why does he judge Babylon for what it did to them?

The chapter answers the question itself. God gave his people into Babylon's hand, but Babylon showed them no mercy and acted from pride, with no thought of serving God's justice. Scripture draws this line often. A nation can be the instrument of judgment and still be accountable for its own motives and its own cruelty, as Assyria was judged in Isaiah 10. God's use of a power does not make everything that power does right.

The judgment on Judah that the chapter mentions is never a reason to blame the Jewish people, and it is not a key for calling any people's suffering deserved. The chapter's own verdict falls on the power that had no mercy.
passages.asks: Babylon thought no one could see what it did. Ask where you have acted as though no one saw. And ask whether your security rests on something that could be taken in a single day.

passages.happening:
‘So take your stand with your spells and with your many sorceries, with which you have wearied yourself from your youth’ (verse 12). The prophet mocks her. Perhaps they will help her; perhaps she will inspire terror (verse 12).

‘You are wearied by your many counselors; let them come forward now and save you’ (verse 13), her astrologers who watch the stars and predict her fate month by month.

‘Surely they are like stubble; the fire will burn them up’ (verse 14). They cannot rescue even themselves from the flame. This is no hearth fire to sit beside and warm the hands (verse 14). Those she traded with from her youth wander off, each his own way. ‘Not one of them can save you’ (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
Babylon was famous across the ancient world for its learned diviners. Its scholars gathered great collections of omens read from the sky, from the livers of sacrificed sheep and from strange events. Court astrologers watched the heavens and reported to the king, above all at the new moon, when the signs for the month were read. Spells and incantations were used to turn disaster away.

The prophet speaks to this whole system as the city's defense and calls it useless. The law of Moses had forbidden these arts in Israel. Here they are shown to be not only forbidden but useless. The experts who claimed to read the future could not see the fire coming for them.

The last verse names the merchants and partners Babylon had dealt with all its life. In the end they scatter. The great trading city is left alone.
passages.later: The law forbade Israel anyone who ‘practices divination or conjury, interprets omens, practices sorcery’ (Deuteronomy 18:10). When Babylon's wise men could not tell Nebuchadnezzar his dream, Daniel said that ‘no wise man, enchanter, medium, or magician can explain to the king the mystery’ (Daniel 2:27).
passages.asks: Babylon wore itself out with counselors and forecasts. Ask where you go for certainty about the future, and whether it can save you. And ask what it would mean to rest in the God who declares the end from the beginning instead.
